narrative:
The system estimates there’s a 50% chance you’ll leave your job in the near future—well above the 40% threshold that triggers caution. Because of this elevated risk, the promotion was denied.

The single biggest factor keeping you in the current role is your relatively short total work history. Employees with more years of experience tend to stay longer, and your 1–5 years of overall experience is below the typical range for those who were promoted. On the other hand, the model sees two strong signals that you may leave soon. First, you’ve received other job offers while working here, which is uncommon among employees who were granted promotions. Second, you work in a sector that historically shows higher turnover than the medical or education fields where most promoted employees are based.

Other aspects of your profile also raised concerns. You’re not satisfied with your wages relative to your effort, you feel physically stressed, and you report psychological exhaustion—all of which are more pronounced than in the group that received promotions. While you’ve benefited from training and feel recognized, these positives weren’t enough to offset the risk flags.

To improve your chances next time, focus on deepening your roots in the organization. Staying longer in your current role and avoiding new job offers would strengthen your case. Addressing wage satisfaction and workplace stress could also help demonstrate your commitment.
